title: When Cognitive Dissonance Becomes Cognitive Offloading
author: Jed Wallace
summary: Jed Wallace of CharterFolk links New York's retreat from academic measures, criticized by the Washington Post editorial board, to a broader failure to know how schools are performing, which he calls society cognitively offloading its own responsibility to know. He then turns to Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay with empathy, describing the cognitive dissonance any parent faces when evidence suggests a choice did not serve their child. Wallace's central criticism is that her long treatment of segregation and opportunity in New York City never mentions charter schools. Using regressions run with an AI assistant, he shows that Black charter students in New York are far more likely than Black district students to attend schools in the top tenth of adjusted performance, with much higher raw proficiency. He argues that the charter cap prevents these schools from meeting demand, and that pushing such evidence out of view turns dissonance into offloading.
points: Wallace argues many states lack comparable data for grades 9 and 10 and for learning before third grade.
Parenting is presented as the domain where cognitive dissonance is most powerful.
About 43 percent of Black charter student records fall in the statewide top adjusted-performance tenth, versus about 13 percent in district schools.
Black charter students posted roughly 68 percent ELA and 69 percent math proficiency, compared with 47 and 43 percent in district schools.
New York City's charter cap blocks growth of the schools producing the strongest results for Black students.
quotes: At the very same moment that understanding the skill levels of young people independent of AI systems is becoming paramount – so that we can know whether our teenagers are engaging in cognitive offloading – society is choosing to cognitively offload our own responsibility to know.
We make choices for our children believing – needing to believe, really – that we are doing right by them.
Because amid a very long examination of segregation, attendance boundaries, selective admissions and the ways families with means secure better educational opportunity, one word never appears:

There is an entire public-school movement in New York City serving very large numbers of Black and economically disadvantaged children, without academically screening them, and producing dramatically different academic results.
The very schools generating those results are effectively subject to a moratorium on meaningful growth under New York City’s charter cap.

And when the discomfort created by that realization becomes so great that we push the evidence out of view – when the R-squareds are sitting in front of us and we refuse to grapple with what they reveal – that is when cognitive dissonance becomes cognitive offloading.
